## Overview

Kumaonis, also known as Kumaiye and Kumain in Nepal, are an Indo-Aryan ethnolinguistic group whose first language is Kumaoni. They live mostly in Kumaon division of Uttarakhand in India; the language is also spoken in the distant northwestern Sudurpashchim Province of Nepal, and Kumaoni speakers are reportedly found in Western Nepal. In 2011, India’s census reported 2,081,057 Kumaoni speakers, including 1,981,062 in Kumaon division. Kumaoni is written in the Devanagari script and belongs to the Central Pahari group within the Indo-Aryan dialect continuum. The sources document clothing, food, festivals, dance, music, theatre, language preservation, and historical inscriptions.

## Material culture

### Textile & pattern traditions

**Pichhaura** — *Pichhaura* is a traditional attire of Kumaoni women, generally worn for religious occasions, marriage, and other rituals. It was traditionally handmade using vegetable dyes and is available in red and saffron; local designs made in Almora, Haldwani, and other parts of Kumaon use silk and accessories made of pearl. The sources state that it is now made using machines.

No named motifs are provided by the sources.

### Clothing & dress

Women’s ceremonial clothing includes the *pichhaura*, worn for religious occasions, marriage, and other rituals. It is associated with red and saffron colours, vegetable dyes, silk, and pearl accessories. Kumaoni men wear the black Kumaoni cap. White Kumaoni caps are worn during festivals, especially during Kumaoni Holi.

### Jewelry & body adornment

The sources mention pearl accessories used with local *pichhaura* designs.

## Music & performance

Kumaoni folk song genres include ceremonial mandals, martial panwaras, and melancholy khuded, thadya, and jhoda. Instruments used in Kumaon music include the dhol, damoun, turri, ransingha, dholki, daur, thali, bhankora, and masakbhaja; tabla and harmonium are also used, but to a lesser extent.

Mohan Upreti is described as the most famous personality associated with Kumaoni folk music. He is known for his Nanda Devi Jagar and Rajula Malu Shahi Ballad, and for the Kumaoni song **Bedu Pako Baro Masa**, which was identified for many years with the hills of Uttarakhand. The sources say that the song was also a favourite of Pandit Jawahar Lal Nehru and was heard in a band march. Mohan Upreti and Naima Upreti sang folk songs as a duet and made the first His Master’s Voice recordings of songs including **Bedu Pako** and **O Lali, O Lali Haushiya**.

Gopal Babu Goswami is described as a legend in Kumaon for his melodious voice. His songs about members of the armed forces and their families include **Kaile baje muruli** and **Ghughuti na basa**. Heera Singh Rana is identified as a contemporary poet and singer whose work addresses hill life, women, beauty, love, romance, suffering, and political satire.

The sources also describe radio initiatives. In 1962, Akashwani Lucknow introduced **Utterayana** for the Chinese border area. TERI launched **Kumaon vani**, a community radio service, on 11 March 2010, and the station covered a radius of 10 km around Mukhteshwar. An internet radio service named **Bedu Pako Baro Masa** was launched in 2008 by non-resident Uttarakhandi people from New York.

## Dance & theatre

**Chholiya** is a popular dance in the Kumaon region and is described as the oldest folk-dance of Uttarakhand. **Jhoda** and **Chanchari** are also identified as folk dances of Kumaon.

Kumaoni theatre developed through *Ramleela* plays and later evolved into a modern theatre form through the efforts of Mohan Upreti, Dinesh Pandey, Naima Khan Upreti, and groups including **Parvatiya Kala Kendra** and **Parvatiya Lok Kala Manch**. Kumaoni Ramlila is associated with the Almora or Kumaon style. The sources state that it is based on the musical rendering of the story of Rama and that its theatrical traditions were set by Uday Shankar during his stay in Almora and later enriched by Mohan Upreti and Brijendra Lal Sah.

## Festivals & rituals

Kumaoni festivals are connected with harvesting, seasonal transitions, the movement of the sun from one constellation to another, and lunar dates. After the harvesting season, people relax, rejoice, dance, and sing, and a festival is generated. Each Sankranti has a fair or festival connected with it somewhere in Kumaon.

The most-observed Sankranties include **Fooldeyi**, **Bikhauti**, **Harela**, **Ghee Sankranti**, **Khatarua**, and **Ghughutiya**. Other auspicious occasions whose dates change frequently in the Gregorian Calendar include **Basant Panchami**, **Shiv Ratri**, **Saton–Athon**, **Kumauni Holi**, **Uttarayani**, **Samvatsar Parwa**, **Ram Navami**, **Dashra**, **Batsavitri**, **Rakshabandhan**, **Janmastmi**, **Nandastmi**, and **Deepawali**.

The sources discuss **Dasshera** in connection with Kumaoni Ramlila. The festival starts in Kumaon with the performance of Ramlila, described as unique because it uses a musical rendering of the story of Rama. The Kumaoni Ramlila is described as 150 years old and was declared by UNESCO to be the longest running opera in the world. The sources also state that the Almora or Kumaon style of Ramlila has been recognised by UNESCO as one of the representative styles of Ramlila in India.

## Foodways

Kumaoni food is described as simple and nutritious, suited to the harsh environment of the Himalayas. It comprises largely vegetables and pulses. Vegetables grown locally include potato, radish, colocasia leaves, pumpkin, and spinach. The sources give the vernacular names *aaloo*, *mooli*, *arbi ke patte*, *papad*, *kaddoo*, and *palak*.

Pulses and cereals are central to the cuisine. *Gouhat*, also called *kulath*, is a local type of bean used in different preparations, including **Kumaoni raitaa**, **Bal Mithai**, **ras bhaat**, **chain**, **faanda**, and **thatwaani**. The sources describe these as unique preparations from the same pulse. **Jholi** is a curry seasoned with curd. **Chudkani** and **Joula** are made from bhatt pulses. Cereals such as *madua*, together with rice and wheat, are popular.

Meat is also prepared, but the recipe is described as similar to preparation in most of North India, with a thinner gravy. Several snack items, breads, dairy products, and beverages form part of Kumaoni cuisine, which is traditionally eaten in several parts of Uttarakhand.

## Oral tradition & literature

The sources mention the musical rendering of the story of Rama in Kumaoni Ramlila and identify the **Rajula Malu Shahi Ballad** as a work associated with Mohan Upreti. They also document folk songs including **Bedu Pako Baro Masa**, **O Lali, O Lali Haushiya**, **Kaile baje muruli**, and **Ghughuti na basa**.

Kumaoni theatre developed through *Ramleela* plays. The language has also been used in plays including **mee yo gayun, mee yo satkyun**, **Punturi**, **Motor Road**, **Labh Ribhadi**, **Kagare Aag**, **Tumhare Liye**, and **कुमाउनी नाटक-जैल थै, वील पै**. The sources name Nand Kumar Upreti, Charu Chandra Pandey, Govind Ballabh Pant, Himanshu Joshi, and Naveeen Joshi in connection with these works.

Kumaoni literature includes writers such as Lokratna Pant, also known as Gumani Pant; Gauri Dutt Pant, known as “Gaurda”; Charu Chandra Pandey; Shailesh Matiyani; Mohan Upreti; and Brijen Lal Shah.

## Language & religion

Kumaoni is an Indo-Aryan language spoken in Kumaon and in the distant northwestern Sudurpashchim Province of Nepal. It is written in the Devanagari script. Dialects identified by the sources include Kali, or Central, Kumaoni in Almora and northern Nainital; North-eastern Kumaoni in Pithoragarh; South-eastern Kumaoni in south-eastern Nainital; and Western Kumaoni west of Almora and Nainital.

Kumaoni shares grammatical features with Indo-Aryan languages including Dotyali, Nepali, Hindi, Rajasthani, Kashmiri, and Gujarati, and with Garhwali of the Central Pahari group. Texts have been found on temple stones and copper plate inscriptions from the Katyuri and Chand era, and Kumaoni was the official language of the Kumaon Kingdom.

The sources state that worship of Vishnu and Shiva is predominant in the region. According to the Skanda Purana, Kumaon is believed to be the birthplace of the Kurma avatar of the Hindu god Vishnu. UNESCO’s Atlas of the World’s Languages in Danger places Kumaoni in the unsafe category, requiring consistent conservation efforts. In December 2019, the government of the state introduced Official Kumaoni Books for Classes 1–5 students in Kumaon division schools.
